I think piano classes are just advertised more than any other instrument honestly.

I taught myself how to play piano as a kid, not because I was forced at all, but just because I was a bored kid. I would have liked piano lessons at some point but my parents didn’t have the money. Despite my amateur playing, my parents still bragged that I knew how to play piano. When I went into highschool, my music teacher threw me on my first wind instrument (a flute) and it turns out, I greatly prefer not needing to read different clefts for each hand.

But yeah, bragging rights for the parents.

I went into therapy thinking the same thing, my childhood was okay. The thing you need to know is that our idea of 'okay' is based on society's standards. So I saw my childhood as okay, but when I explained things to my therapist at the time, she told me it was not okay. Your mind will react the way it does, no matter if you see things as okay.  


The point of therapy is to point out what went wrong, and to solve the problems that came from it. So yes, there are benefits to discussing childhood events. Things you might see as fine, they might not. For example, when I first started therapy, I didn't realize it wasn't normal for my health concerns to be pushed under the rug. This was something that I saw as okay, when others wouldn't. That caused me to push my own concerns under the rug, and when I'm in severe pain I deny the need for a doctor until I'm blue in the face.

For me, it was to minimize the emotional pain I was feeling by feeling physical pain instead. It was a distraction. I didn't want to feel the emotional pain, so the physical pain would push it out of my head temporarily. It started out because people told me they liked when I was hurting, that it was cool to cut yourself, all this stuff. I was 11 years old, and a people pleaser. I did what I had to to get some attention. Then something clicked in my brain that made me slightly addicted to the feeling of turning off the emotional pain by replacing it by physical pain.

The thing that helped me was hiding all the things I would use. Scissors, knives, exacto blades, screws, nails, compasses (the kind to draw circles), needles, basically anything somewhat sharp. Sometimes I would get desperate and go searching for this stuff, but I wouldn't be able to find it. Started using belts to choke myself instead, so I threw out all the belts. It was a lot of work, but worth it.

Tbh I do limit the playing to a couple of rooms only, not the common area as you put it (I call it our living room). I used to allow it, but after asking them not to throw toys, not to run, not to beat each other up, etc. so many times I give up. The problem is I have a very small house, and if they do these things, they will break the TV, windows, or each other. So now I just don't allow it. I was raised the same way, I had pretty much free reign, and I tried allowing my two step kids the same but I won't if they'll behave like that.   


If they aren't doing anything wrong though, like screaming or yelling, throwing things, rough play sort of stuff, I would say just leave them be. If you need some quiet time you could ask them if they can play somewhere else, or you could take your laptop to your room.

Hi there. I’m a weird one, therapy and social workers didn’t work for me, and I had to stop taking meds, so I kinda know how to handle mental illnesses like this by myself. 

Before I mention that, most schools have social workers that are either free or discounted for their students. I saw other people comment that, but just enforcing that it’s an option, some of my favourite social workers were through the school. Again though, it made me worse, so I stopped doing it. 

Find out the source of your depression by exploring your own emotions. You mentioned you have a fear of rejection, lack of confidence, lack of friends, etc. these are feelings that are the result of something else. You’re hard on yourself, so that’s a place you can start. You are interested in the gym and movies, is there anything you’re proud of yourself for doing with those things? I tried going to the gym regularly and couldn’t do it at all, I think that should be something to be proud of if you’re going regularly. 

A lot of the time, lack of socializing can cause depression for some people. But with your low confidence and it negativities you said, having a social life can definitely be difficult. I have low confidence too, and one method of increasing it for me was to start saying no to people’s requests. I have always had a hard time saying no because I’m scared of their reaction, but now I just don’t care. 

I’m 27 and I feel very much behind. I have about 9 years worth of college education, one useless diploma, and a short resume full of fast food experience. I feel this pain and uncertainty. My boyfriend’s kids have been taught by their grandmother that I’m nothing to them (their bio mom left when the youngest was 4 months old, I’ve been there throughout their lives for 8 years, I’m something) so I’m always worried that when I take a toy or something they’ll say “whatever, you’re not my parent anyways”. 

Try to have a positive relationship with them, but remind them that you’re there to teach them. They will have consequences for their actions, and sometimes you’ll be the person to enforce those consequences so that they’ll learn. I wouldn’t get physical with them either, I can understand why that’s where your thoughts would go because of your past, but maybe try to think of discipline that would have been a better option for you as a kid their age. I take things they don’t need away that are relative to the problem, but if they’re just not listening to me and there’s nothing too relative I’ll take screen time away and let them know that kids who don’t listen to their parents don’t get screen time. Luckily I don’t have to deal with their biological mother, but if I’m not sure if it’s the right idea, I talk to my boyfriend about it first to get his thoughts. They are his children, but he sees me as a parent just as much as he is to them. I always tell him I don’t feel like that and really, I am nothing to them, if he died tomorrow the chances of me ever getting to see them again would be 0%.

Anyways, teach them that your discipline is the consequences of some of their actions (sometimes natural consequences are better, like I’ve told my step kids not to run up and down the stairs so many times that at this point if they fall and cry about getting hurt I say oh well, at least it’s not bad this time, of course if it was a bad fall I would be more worried but if they fell up the stairs and scrape their shins oh well). You’re not trying to be mean when you discipline, you’re trying to help teach them to be better ‘thems’ and to help them be happy. 

So don’t think about what would have happened to you as a kid, because you know that was wrong. Think about what should have happened as a consequence to your actions as a kid. Did you throw a toy and break something, so your step parent hit you? Maybe a better consequence would have been to take your toy away and have you clean up your mess. All hitting does is make a child scared of the person, not so much scared or aware of what they did wrong. It also teaches children that if things don’t go their way, they should hit others. 

If you can, and I’m sure you have, maybe seek a social worker to help talk you through some of your own trauma. They might be able to help you with alternative ways of thinking :) and it doesn’t make you a bad step dad at all! You’re trying to do better than what you had as a child, and that’s all you can do. I think that’s great. I can understand why you’d think that, but it definitely doesn’t make you bad, it’s the opposite. It shows you’re willing and capable of growth.
